IPv6

The router takes IPv6 from the provider on its internet-facing interfaces: an address (SLAAC or DHCPv6) and, if the provider delegates one, a prefix. Each LAN zone's interface gets a /64 network of that prefix, which its devices configure themselves from (SLAAC; ipv6.lan_zones chooses the zones, all of them by default). Each also gets a stable network of the router's own (ULA), where the router answers DNS whatever the provider gives. The rules decide what the LAN reaches over IPv6, as over IPv4; nothing new comes in from the internet but through a pinhole (ipv6.pinholes). The webUI and SSH answer over IPv6 only with management.ipv6, on the stable address.

The router takes IPv6 from the provider on its internet-facing interfaces: an address (SLAAC or DHCPv6) and, if the provider delegates one, a prefix. Each LAN zone's interface gets a /64 network of that prefix, which its devices configure themselves from (SLAAC; ipv6.lan_zones chooses the zones, all of them by default). Each also gets a stable network of the router's own (ULA), where the router answers DNS whatever the provider gives. The rules decide what the LAN reaches over IPv6, as over IPv4; nothing new comes in from the internet but through a pinhole (ipv6.pinholes). The webUI and SSH answer over IPv6 only with management.ipv6, on the stable address.

IPv6

The router takes IPv6 from the provider on its internet-facing interfaces: an address (SLAAC or DHCPv6) and, if the provider delegates one, a prefix. Each LAN zone's interface gets a /64 network of that prefix, which its devices configure themselves from (SLAAC; ipv6.lan_zones chooses the zones, all of them by default). Each also gets a stable network of the router's own (ULA), where the router answers DNS whatever the provider gives. The rules decide what the LAN reaches over IPv6, as over IPv4; nothing new comes in from the internet but through a pinhole (ipv6.pinholes). The webUI and SSH answer over IPv6 only with management.ipv6, on the stable address.

FR_OSProtectionTLS SNI Filter

XDP TLS SNI Filter

Kernel-space (XDP/eBPF) TLS ClientHello inspection -- drops connections to blocklisted domains before they reach the kernel's normal network stack. What it can't see is listed below, and in bpf/xdp_sni_filter.c -- read that before relying on this as a complete filter.

Disabled
Interface
-
Blocked domains
0
Drops (since last load)

What this filter doesn't see

  • QUIC (HTTP/3, UDP/443). Its ClientHello is encrypted. Rejected from the filtered ports and their VLANs once the filter is on and applied.
  • Encrypted Client Hello (ECH). The real name is encrypted; the filter sees only the outer, public one.
  • TLS on ports other than 443.
  • ClientHellos over several TLS records. They pass, counted as truncated. One split across TCP segments is followed: a segment out of order is dropped until TCP sends it in order, one with a bad checksum is dropped unread, and a hello longer than 16 segments, unfinished after 30 seconds or in a segment over 2,048 bytes is dropped.
  • Names of 32 bytes or more. Refused when you add them, so none is silently ineffective.
  • IPv6 with more than four extension headers, and TCP fragments. The filter reads IPv6 like IPv4, behind up to four extension headers. A packet with more, and a TCP fragment of either family, is dropped instead: no LAN device sends one, and the server would put a hello back together that the filter never saw whole.

Settings

XDP only sees packets an interface receives. To filter what LAN clients connect to, pick the LAN-side interfaces; on the WAN interface it only sees connections coming in from the internet.

Blocking a domain also blocks its subdomains (e.g. "example.com" blocks "www.example.com" too) -- see this project's ARCHITECTURE.md for the LPM-trie matching scheme.

Saving only updates config.yaml -- click Apply on the dashboard to actually load the filter into the kernel.

Blocked domains

No domains configured yet.

Streamed from fr-xdp-sni-logger's journal as each match is logged -- the drop decision itself already happened in the kernel, entirely independent of this page being open. "40Gbps wire-speed" describes what the native (xdpdrv) data plane is designed for on supported hardware, not a throughput number measured on this box -- see ROADMAP.md's phase 4 open items for real hardware benchmarking status. FR_OSNetworkSegments

Network segments

On one flat network, a hacked camera or a guest's infected laptop can reach every other device. A segment is a separate network with its own addresses and DHCP that can reach the internet and nothing else. Each one here is a VLAN on the LAN port (?): set your access point to put the IoT and guest Wi-Fi on these VLAN IDs (or use a VLAN-capable switch).

SegmentVLANNetworkDevice
IoT devices (iot) 30 192.168.30.1/24 -
Guests (guest) 40 192.168.40.1/24 -

Each gets DHCP (.100-.199, public DNS), a rule to the internet and nothing towards your LAN or this router's management. IoT devices are also inventoried and isolated (see IoT Devices).

Firewall rules

Evaluated in order, first match wins. "self" as a zone means the router itself. Scheduled drop/reject rules that cut open connections are evaluated before all other rules.

Rule check

No problems found -- no any-to-any or internet-wide accept rules, nothing shadowed, nothing unused for 90 days.

Rule hit counters are recorded hourly (fr-schedule-check.timer); "unused" means no match for 90 days.

No day ticked = every day. An end time before the start runs past midnight (22:00-06:00).

TLS Fingerprints

Identifies which TLS software each device uses -- browser, app, library or script -- from the unencrypted first message of every TLS connection (the ClientHello), without decrypting anything. JA4 is stable per client software (the recommended one); JA3 is shown too, but browsers that shuffle their extensions produce a new JA3 on almost every connection.

FR_OSProtectionApplications

Applications

Recognises which apps clients use from the names they look up through the router's resolver and, optionally, the TLS server names (SNI) the XDP filter sees -- nothing is decrypted. A "hit" is one lookup or one TLS connection, a rough activity signal, not traffic volume. Apps are blocked by the resolver answering "no such domain" for all of their names.

Settings

Prerequisites

  • off DNS observation: Ad-Block resolver enabled with query logging
  • off DNS blocking: Ad-Block resolver announced to LAN clients (serve_lan)
  • off Clients cannot bypass the resolver with their own DNS server (force_dns)
  • off SNI observation: XDP filter enabled on the LAN-side interfaces with observe_sni

Daemon fr-appid: not running . The XDP filter only sees what an interface receives: attach it to the LAN-side interfaces, not the WAN. It also misses names of 32 characters or more, QUIC (HTTP/3) and Encrypted Client Hello.

Downloads blocklists (hosts files or plain domain lists), dedupes them, and serves the result from a dedicated, frfw-managed DNS resolver (dnsmasq). Each category is kept as its own list, so blocks and counts can be told apart. Optionally also pushes a small "critical" subset of the base list into the existing Phase 4 XDP kernel filter.

request.yaml:
version: 1
hostname: edge-gw
interfaces:
  wan:
    device: eth0
    zone: wan
  lan:
    device: eth1
    zone: lan
    address: 192.168.1.1/24
  iot:
    device: eth2
    zone: iot
    address: 192.168.20.1/24
zones:
  wan: {}
  lan: {}
  iot: {}
nat:
  masquerade:
  - out_zone: wan
dhcp:
  lan:
    range_start: 192.168.1.100
    range_end: 192.168.1.200
    dns_servers:
    - 192.168.1.1
    reservations:
    - mac: aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:10
      address: 192.168.1.10
rules:
- name: lan-to-wan
  action: accept
  from_zone: lan
  to_zone: wan
adblocker:
  enabled: true
  source_urls:
  - https://lists.example/hosts
  serve_lan: true
  query_logging: true
  categories:
    malware:
    - https://lists.example/malware
    my-list:
    - https://lists.example/mine
    - https://lists.example/mine2
  allowlist:
  - ok.example
local_dns:
  domain: lan
  hosts:
    nas.lan: 192.168.1.10
    printer.lan: 192.168.1.11
    server.lan: 192.168.1.13
  overrides:
    intranet.example: 192.168.1.12
ai_ids:
  enabled: true
  excluded_macs:
  - aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:10
  quarantine_duration_seconds: 900
tls_fingerprint:
  enabled: true
  blocklist:
  - fingerprint: t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_e5627efa2ab1
    label: old curl
  - 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
xdp_sni_filter:
  enabled: true
  interfaces:
  - lan
  - iot
  blocklist:
  - ads.example.com
  - tracker.example.net
app_control:
  enabled: true
  observe_sni: true
  blocked_apps:
  - tiktok
iot:
  enabled: true
  zones:
  - iot
  auto_isolate: true
  trusted_macs:
  - aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02
  isolated_macs:
  - aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:03

FR_OSProtectionTLS SNI Filter

XDP TLS SNI Filter

Kernel-space (XDP/eBPF) TLS ClientHello inspection -- drops connections to blocklisted domains before they reach the kernel's normal network stack. What it can't see is listed below, and in bpf/xdp_sni_filter.c -- read that before relying on this as a complete filter.

Not attached yet -- run Apply
Interface
lan, iot
Blocked domains
2
Drops (since last load)
unavailable -- the apply-helper didn't answer; firewall-cli xdp-status shows them

What this filter doesn't see

  • QUIC (HTTP/3, UDP/443). Its ClientHello is encrypted. Rejected from eth1, eth2 while the filter is on, so browsers fall back to TLS over TCP, where the name is seen.
  • Encrypted Client Hello (ECH). The real name is encrypted; the filter sees only the outer, public one.
  • TLS on ports other than 443.
  • ClientHellos over several TLS records. They pass, counted as truncated. One split across TCP segments is followed: a segment out of order is dropped until TCP sends it in order, one with a bad checksum is dropped unread, and a hello longer than 16 segments, unfinished after 30 seconds or in a segment over 2,048 bytes is dropped.
  • Names of 32 bytes or more. Refused when you add them, so none is silently ineffective.
  • IPv6 with more than four extension headers, and TCP fragments. The filter reads IPv6 like IPv4, behind up to four extension headers. A packet with more, and a TCP fragment of either family, is dropped instead: no LAN device sends one, and the server would put a hello back together that the filter never saw whole.

Settings

XDP only sees packets an interface receives. To filter what LAN clients connect to, pick the LAN-side interfaces; on the WAN interface it only sees connections coming in from the internet.

Blocking a domain also blocks its subdomains (e.g. "example.com" blocks "www.example.com" too) -- see this project's ARCHITECTURE.md for the LPM-trie matching scheme.

Saving only updates config.yaml -- click Apply on the dashboard to actually load the filter into the kernel.

Identifies which TLS software each device uses -- browser, app, library or script -- from the unencrypted first message of every TLS connection (the ClientHello), without decrypting anything. JA4 is stable per client software (the recommended one); JA3 is shown too, but browsers that shuffle their extensions produce a new JA3 on almost every connection.

Ad-Block & DNS Filtering

Downloads blocklists (hosts files or plain domain lists), dedupes them, and serves the result from a dedicated, frfw-managed DNS resolver (dnsmasq). Each category is kept as its own list, so blocks and counts can be told apart. Optionally also pushes a small "critical" subset of the base list into the existing Phase 4 XDP kernel filter.

Disabled
Domains loaded
0
ads
0

Base list

Suggested: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/StevenBlack/hosts/master/hosts

Feeds up to this many base-list domains into the existing TLS SNI filter's kernel blocklist -- only takes effect if that filter is also enabled; leave at 0 to keep everything DNS-side.

Categories

Each list's own license and terms apply -- check them before use in a business.

LAN DNS

Local names

Names the router's resolver answers itself, for the clients it serves (needs Enabled and "Serve DHCP clients" above). A host is one exact name; an override also covers every subdomain, e.g. an internal server for a public name. They are never sent upstream and never blocked.

No local names yet.

Refresh

Downloads and dedupes the configured lists right now, instead of waiting for the daily fr-adblock-refresh.timer. Can take a while depending on list size and network speed.

XDP TLS SNI Filter

Kernel-space (XDP/eBPF) TLS ClientHello inspection -- drops connections to blocklisted domains before they reach the kernel's normal network stack. What it can't see is listed below, and in bpf/xdp_sni_filter.c -- read that before relying on this as a complete filter.

Native / Driver (xdpdrv)
Interface
lan
Blocked domains
2
Drops (since last load)
17

Attached interfaces

InterfaceDeviceMode
lan eth1 Native / Driver (xdpdrv)
iot eth2 Generic / SKB (xdpgeneric)

What this filter doesn't see

  • QUIC (HTTP/3, UDP/443). Its ClientHello is encrypted. Rejected from eth1, eth2 while the filter is on, so browsers fall back to TLS over TCP, where the name is seen.
  • Encrypted Client Hello (ECH). The real name is encrypted; the filter sees only the outer, public one.
  • TLS on ports other than 443.
  • ClientHellos over several TLS records. They pass, counted as truncated. One split across TCP segments is followed: a segment out of order is dropped until TCP sends it in order, one with a bad checksum is dropped unread, and a hello longer than 16 segments, unfinished after 30 seconds or in a segment over 2,048 bytes is dropped.
  • Names of 32 bytes or more. Refused when you add them, so none is silently ineffective.
  • IPv6 with more than four extension headers, and TCP fragments. The filter reads IPv6 like IPv4, behind up to four extension headers. A packet with more, and a TCP fragment of either family, is dropped instead: no LAN device sends one, and the server would put a hello back together that the filter never saw whole.

Settings

XDP only sees packets an interface receives. To filter what LAN clients connect to, pick the LAN-side interfaces; on the WAN interface it only sees connections coming in from the internet.

Blocking a domain also blocks its subdomains (e.g. "example.com" blocks "www.example.com" too) -- see this project's ARCHITECTURE.md for the LPM-trie matching scheme.

Saving only updates config.yaml -- click Apply on the dashboard to actually load the filter into the kernel.

  • IPv6 with more than four extension headers, and TCP fragments. The filter reads IPv6 like IPv4, behind up to four extension headers. A packet with more, and a TCP fragment of either family, is dropped instead: no LAN device sends one, and the server would put a hello back together that the filter never saw whole.

Settings

XDP only sees packets an interface receives. To filter what LAN clients connect to, pick the LAN-side interfaces; on the WAN interface it only sees connections coming in from the internet.

Blocking a domain also blocks its subdomains (e.g. "example.com" blocks "www.example.com" too) -- see this project's ARCHITECTURE.md for the LPM-trie matching scheme.

Saving only updates config.yaml -- click Apply on the dashboard to actually load the filter into the kernel.

FR_OSNetworkSegments

Network segments

On one flat network, a hacked camera or a guest's infected laptop can reach every other device. A segment is a separate network with its own addresses and DHCP that can reach the internet and nothing else. Each one here is a VLAN on the LAN port (eth1): set your access point to put the IoT and guest Wi-Fi on these VLAN IDs (or use a VLAN-capable switch).

SegmentVLANNetworkDevice
IoT devices (iot) 30 192.168.30.1/24 eth1.30 set up
Guests (guest) 40 192.168.40.1/24 eth1.40 set up

Each gets DHCP (.100-.199, public DNS), a rule to the internet and nothing towards your LAN or this router's management. IoT devices are also inventoried and isolated (see IoT Devices).
